problems.title: Treasure Hunting
problems.problem:
After he beat Tanaka in last year's cook-off contest (yes, the most important contest in all of Info(1)Cup Kingdom), Lulu decided to quit cooking and go *treasure hunting*. But since Tanaka is a very ambitious person, he wants to get his revenge and beat Lulu this time. The hunt takes place inside of a maze which can be represented as a matrix of size $n \times m$. Each cell $(x, y)$ can be either a wall (represented by the character `#`) or a treasure cell (represented by the character `$`). Each treasure cell can contain at most one treasure. Initially, all treasure cells contain a treasure.

We say that the cell $(x', y')$ is reachable from $(x, y)$ if one can get from $(x, y)$ to $(x', y')$ by moving only *down* or to the *right* through treasure cells. Note that a treasure cell is reachable from itself.

**The maze has a very interesting property.** The cell $(n, m)$ is reachable from any treasure cell and any treasure cell is reachable from $(1, 1)$. Let $F(x, y)$ be the number of treasure cells which contain a treasure and can be reached from $(x, y)$. We define $F(x, y) = 0$ if $(x, y)$ is a wall. Tanaka thinks that he could get ahead of his opponent by finding $S$, the sum of $F(x, y)$ for all $1 \le x \le n$ and $1 \le y \le m$, i.e.

$$S = \sum_{x=1}^{n} \sum_{y=1}^{m} F(x, y)$$

But then the real treasure hunt begins! At each moment, one of two things can happen:

• 1. The cell $(x, y)$ gets an update. If the cell previously had a treasure in it, then the treasure disappears. Otherwise, a treasure appears in the cell $(x, y)$.
• 2. Tanaka wants to know $F(x, y)$ for a given cell $(x, y)$.

Tanaka doesn't have enough time to do all this on his own, so he needs your programming skills. Help Tanaka beat Lulu by writing a program which calculates the value $S$, then answers all of his queries right.

## Input data

The first line of input contains the integers $n$, $m$ and $Q$, the number of rows and columns in the matrix and the number of operations you need to process. The next $n$ lines contain $m$ characters, representing the maze. Each of the next $Q$ lines contains an operation, which will be represented as follows:

• `! x y`, which means the cell $(x, y)$ gets an update.
• `? x y`, which means you have to output the value $F(x, y)$.

It is guaranteed that $(x, y)$ is a treasure cell in both cases.

## Output data

The first line of output must contain the value $S$, the sum of $F(x, y)$ for all cells $(x, y)$ in the initial state. Each of the next lines must contain the answers to Tanaka's queries, in order.

## Restrictions

• $1 \le n, m \le 1\,000$
• $1 \le Q \le 50\,000$

Gregor lives by the saying "One for all and all for one", so you can('t) imagine what he has done when he received a sequence of $N$ numbers for his birthday! For example, if the sequence contains the integers $1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3$, then applying the operation for $x = 1$ yields $2, 2, 3, 3, 2, 2, 3, 3$.

Gregor would like you to apply this operation a number of times so that the resulting sequence has certain properties. First, the resulting sequence must be *increasing*, and second, among all such increasing sequences, it must have *maximum length*. We consider a sequence $a_1, \ldots, a_N$ to be increasing if $a_1 \le a_2 \le \cdots \le a_N$. Similarly we consider it to be decreasing if $a_1 \ge a_2 \ge \cdots \ge a_N$.

C++ header: `ping-pong.h`

Three friends, Anna, Bob and Charlie, play ping-pong. Ping-pong is a two-player game, so while two of them play the third simply watches. After a game is over, the player who won stays at the table, and then plays with the person who was watching. For example, if Anna beats Bob, then she plays the next match with Charlie.

One day, their informatics teacher asked them the following question. How many ways could the three have played so that Anna wins *exactly* $a$ matches, Bob *exactly* $b$ matches and Charlie *exactly* $c$ matches? Because this can be a very large number, the teacher is satisfied with the answer modulo $10^{9} + 7$.

We now explain when we consider two ways of playing different. For a way of playing $P$, let $\mathrm{Win}(P)$ be the list of players who win each game and $\mathrm{Watch}(P)$ be the list of players who watch each game. Then, two ways of playing $P$ and $Q$ are considered to be different if there is a match $i$ for $1 \le i \le a + b + c$ where $\mathrm{Win}(P)_i \ne \mathrm{Win}(Q)_i$ or $\mathrm{Watch}(P)_i \ne \mathrm{Watch}(Q)_i$.

This question seems pretty difficult for them. Can you help them?

You should implement the following function.

```C++
int solve(int a, int b, int c);
```

This function should return the answer for the given values of $a$, $b$ and $c$. It will only be called *once* per execution by the committee's grader.

You may use the following function while implementing your solution.

```C++
int combinations(int n, int k);
```

This will return in constant time $\binom{n}{k} \bmod 10^{9} + 7$, i.e. the binomial coefficient corresponding to $n, k$, or the number ways of choosing $k$ objects from among $n$ objects, all modulo $10^{9} + 7$. Note that the parameters $n$ and $k$ need to satisfy $0 \le k \le n \le 5\,000\,000$.

problems.title: XORsecv
problems.author: Iulian Arsenoiu, Tudor Mușat, Tamio Vesa-Nakajima
problems.problem:
XORnelius is the greatest mathematician in the Info(1)cup Kingdom. One day he stumbled upon a very interesting algorithmic task. But instead of solving it, which would have been easy for him, he decided to give it to you as a test.

You are given an array $a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_{N-1}$ of numbers. For a contiguous subsequence $(i, j)$ of this array, we calculate the *XORvalue* of the sequence using the following steps:

• 1. We create an array $b$ of size $k = j - i + 1$, so that $b_0 = a_i, b_1 = a_{i+1}, \ldots b_{k-1} = a_j$.
• 2. The XORvalue is equal to the sum of the values $(b_i \mathbin{\mathrm{xor}} i)^{P}$, for all $0 \le i < k$.$^{1}$

Calculate the sum of the XORvalues of all contiguous subsequences of the array, modulo $10^{9} + 7$.

Formally, if we let $f(i, j)$ denote the XORvalue of sequence $(i, j)$, we have that

$$f(i, j) = \sum_{m=0}^{j-i} (a_{i+m} \mathbin{\mathrm{xor}} m)^{P}.$$

You are asked to find the following value

$$\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} \sum_{j=i}^{N-1} f(i, j) \pmod{10^{9} + 7}.$$

Your task is to solve this problem and prove to XORnelius that you are as great of a mathematician as he is.

## Input data

The first line of input contains $N$, denoting the size of the array, and $P$. The second line contains values $a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_{N-1}$.

## Output data

The only line of output must contain the required answer.

## Restrictions

• $1 \le N \le 250\,000$
• $1 \le P \le 1\,000\,000\,000$
• $0 \le a_i < 2^{18}$, for all $0 \le i < N$

$^{1}$ The $\mathrm{xor}$ operator is denoted by `^` in C++. Formally, we define it as follows. For $x, y \in \mathbb{N}$, let $z$ be equal to $x \mathbin{\mathrm{xor}} y$. Then, the $k$-th bit of $z$ is equal to 1 if and only if the $k$-th bit of $x$ is equal to 1 or the $k$-th bit of $y$ is equal to 1, but not both.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|l} \# & \text{Points} & \text{Restrictions} \\ \hline 1 & 7 & N \le 100,\ P = 1 \\ 2 & 8 & N \le 1\,000,\ P = 1 \\ 3 & 12 & N \le 1\,000 \\ 4 & 15 & P = 1 \\ 5 & 12 & N \le 50\,000,\ a_i < 8, \text{ for all } 0 \le i < N \\ 6 & 14 & N \le 50\,000,\ P = 2 \\ 7 & 32 & \text{No further restrictions} \end{array}$$

## Examples

### Example 1

```input
3 3
3 2 4
```

```output
556
```

### Example 2

```input
7 1
4 2 3 6 5 7 11
```

```output
379
```

### Example 3

```input
6 2
1 3 15 7 15 31
```

```output
9410
```

## Explanations

**First example** The XORvalues of all the contiguous subsequences in the array are written below:

• $i = 0, j = 0$: $b = \{3\}$, $f(0, 0) = (3 \mathbin{\mathrm{xor}} 0)^{3} = 3^{3} = 27$
• $i = 0, j = 1$: $b = \{3, 2\}$, $f(0, 1) = (3 \mathbin{\mathrm{xor}} 0)^{3} + (2 \mathbin{\mathrm{xor}} 1)^{3} = 3^{3} + 3^{3} = 27 + 27 = 54$
• $i = 0, j = 2$: $b = \{3, 2, 4\}$, $f(0, 2) = (3 \mathbin{\mathrm{xor}} 0)^{3} + (2 \mathbin{\mathrm{xor}} 1)^{3} + (4 \mathbin{\mathrm{xor}} 2)^{3} = 3^{3} + 3^{3} + 6^{3} = 27 + 27 + 216 = 270$
• $i = 1, j = 1$: $b = \{2\}$, $f(1, 1) = (2 \mathbin{\mathrm{xor}} 0)^{3} = 2^{3} = 8$
• $i = 1, j = 2$: $b = \{2, 4\}$, $f(1, 2) = (2 \mathbin{\mathrm{xor}} 0)^{3} + (4 \mathbin{\mathrm{xor}} 1)^{3} = 2^{3} + 5^{3} = 8 + 125 = 133$
• $i = 2, j = 2$: $b = \{4\}$, $f(2, 2) = (4 \mathbin{\mathrm{xor}} 0)^{3} = 4^{3} = 64$

The sum of all these values is equal to 556 modulo $10^{9} + 7$.

problems.title: Bracket Wheel
problems.author: Predescu Sebastian
problems.problem:
*Money Gold Medals can't buy happiness*

*Certainly not a programmer*

Seby the little square has recently heard about the newest attraction in the Info(1)cup Fair: the bracket wheel! The wheel consists of $n$ parantheses, placed on a circular frame, that can be seen as a sequence of $n$ characters, each of which can either be '(' or ')'. Spinning the wheel is equivalent to transforming it into one of its cyclic shifts.

Now, we define the *cyclic shifts* of a sequence as follows. Given a sequence $a_1, \ldots, a_n$, the sequence has $n$ cyclic shifts: $n - 1$ of form $a_i, \ldots, a_n, a_1, \ldots, a_{i-1}$ when $1 < i \le n$, and one cyclic shift equal to the original sequence $a_1, \ldots, a_n$. For example the sequence of parentheses `()(())` has the following cyclic shifts:

• 1. `()(())`,
• 2. `)(())(`,
• 3. `(())()`,
• 4. `())()(`,
• 5. `))()((`,
• 6. `)()(()`,

We call a sequence of parentheses *balanced* if we can insert 1 and + into the sequence so that it becomes a valid mathematical expression. For example, `(())()` is balanced, since we can insert 1 and + to form $((1 + 1) + 1) + (1 + 1)$, but `)(()` or `(()` are not. More formally, a sequence $a$ is balanced if and only if it is empty or of the form $(b)c$ where $b$ and $c$ are balanced.

Given a sequence of parentheses $s$, we define the *value* of $s$, denoted by $\mathrm{val}(s)$, to be the number of cyclic shifts of $s$ that are balanced. For example, if $s = $ `()(())`, we have $\mathrm{val}(s) = 2$, due to the cyclic shifts `()(())` and `(())()`.

The rules of the game are simple. The player is given $k$ Gold Medals. They can spend one gold medal to swap two parentheses on the wheel. The score of the player is then the number of cyclic shifts of the sequence on the wheel which are balanced. That is, if $s$ is the sequence on the wheel, then the score is $\mathrm{val}(s)$. Can you help Seby spend his $k$ Gold Medals to maximise his score?

Formally, you are given a sequence $s$ of $n$ parentheses, and have the ability to swap $k$ pairs of parentheses within $s$. Find a way to perform these swaps in order to maximize the value of the resulting sequence.

## Input Data

The first line of the input contains the integers $n$ and $k$. The second line of the input contains the sequence $s$ of parentheses.

## Output Data

The output contains the maximum value that could be obtained after performing the swaps.

## Restrictions

• $1 \le n \le 50\,000$
• $0 \le k \le 9$.
• $s$ contains only parentheses i.e. '(' and ')'. It is guaranteed that the number of '(' in $s$ is equal to the number of ')'.
• The number of Gold Medals Seby won is significantly bigger, but his instinct tells him he might need them again in the near future.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|l} \# & \text{Points} & \text{Restrictions} \\ \hline 1 & 7 & n \le 500,\ k = 0 \\ 2 & 9 & n \le 20,\ k = 1 \\ 3 & 13 & n \le 500,\ k = 1 \\ 4 & 17 & k = 0 \\ 5 & 18 & n \le 2\,000,\ k = 1 \\ 6 & 19 & k = 1 \\ 7 & 17 & \text{No further restrictions} \end{array}$$

## Examples

```input
6 1
)(())(
```

```output
3
```

**First example.** In this case, we can swap parantheses on positions 3 and 4. The resulting sequence is `)()()(`, which has the following cyclic shifts:

• 1. `)()()(`
• 2. `()()()`
• 3. `)()()(`
• 4. `()()()`
• 5. `)()()(`
• 6. `()()()`

Out of these, only 3 are balanced sequences.

problems.title: Maxstack
problems.author: Iulian Arsenoiu
problems.problem:
We define the following two operations which can be performed on a stack:

• $\mathrm{push}(x)$ — the number $x$ is added to the top of the stack,
• $\mathrm{pop}$ — the number on top of the stack is removed from the stack.

A sequence of operations is considered to be *correct* if, when the operations are performed on an initially empty stack in order, the following two conditions are met:

• 1. No pop operation is performed on an empty stack,
• 2. After the last operation, the stack is empty.

For example, $(\mathrm{push}(1), \mathrm{pop})$ is correct, whereas $(\mathrm{push}(1), \mathrm{push}(2))$, or $(\mathrm{pop}, \mathrm{push}(1))$ are not.

We will consider a list $L_1, \ldots, L_N$ of operations, numbered from 1 to $N$. By $s(i, j)$, where $i \le j$, we denote the sequence of operations $L_i, L_{i+1}, \ldots, L_j$.

We define the value $\mathrm{maxstack}(i, j)$ as follows. If $s(i, j)$ is not a correct sequence, then we define $\mathrm{maxstack}(i, j) = 0$. Otherwise, we perform the operations $L_i, L_{i+1}, \ldots, L_j$ in order on an initially empty stack. After each operation, we calculate the maximum value in the stack. Let $m_k$ be the maximum value after operation $k$, or zero if the stack is empty. Then, $\mathrm{maxstack}(i, j) = m_i + m_{i+1} + \cdots + m_j$.

You are given $N$, the list $L$ of operations, a number $Q$, and $Q$ queries of the form $(l, r)$, where $1 \le l \le r \le N$. You are also given a number $C$. Depending on the value of $C$, you must calculate the following for all queries:

• 1. If $C = 1$, then you should calculate $\mathrm{maxstack}(l, r)$ modulo $10^{9} + 7$. **It is guaranteed that $s(l, r)$ is correct for all queries.**
• 2. If $C = 2$, then you should calculate the sum of $\mathrm{maxstack}(i, j)$ for all $l \le i \le j \le r$ modulo $10^{9} + 7$. **It is guaranteed that for every query, if you perform the operations of $s(l, r)$ in order, then no pop operation is performed on an empty stack.**

## Input data

The first line of input contains the value $C$. The second line contains the integers $N$ and $Q$. The third line contains non-negative integers $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_N$, which encode $L_1, \ldots, L_N$ as follows:

• If $X_i > 0$, then $L_i = \mathrm{push}(X_i)$,
• If $X_i = 0$, then $L_i = \mathrm{pop}$.

Each of the following $Q$ lines contains two integers $l$ and $r$, representing the queries.

## Output data

Each of the $Q$ lines of output should contain the answers to the queries, in order. All answers must be given modulo $10^{9} + 7$.

## Restrictions

• $1 \le N, Q \le 300\,000$.
• $0 \le X_i \le 10^{9}$, for all $1 \le i \le N$
• $L_1, \ldots, L_N$ is guaranteed to be a correct sequence of operations
• We call a sequence of operations *finally empty* if, when performing these operations on an empty stack, the stack is empty only before the first operation and after the last one. For example, $(\mathrm{push}(1), \mathrm{pop})$ is finally empty, but $(\mathrm{push}(1), \mathrm{pop}, \mathrm{push}(1), \mathrm{pop})$ is not.

$$\mathrm{value}_K(x) = x + 10^{P_K(x)}$$

$$\mathrm{answer}(N, K) = \max_{0 \le x < N} \mathrm{value}_K(x).$$

problems.title: Cards
problems.problem:
Little CS is playing a game which involves a deck of $N$ cards numbered from 1 to $N$ and an initially empty board. Each card has a positive integer value written on it, so that no two cards in the deck have the same value. The game is played as follows:

• 1. Little CS reshuffles the cards so that they are in an order of his choice. Let $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_N$ be the order of the cards in the deck after Little CS reshuffles them, where $p_i$ is the value written on the $i$-th card
• 2. Little CS repeatedly picks the first card in the deck and has two options:
◦ If the card is *dominant*, he then has to place it on the board. A card is considered dominant if either the board is empty or the value written on it is at least twice as big as the value written on any card on the board.
◦ If the card is not dominant, he has to throw it away and cannot use it again.
• 3. When the deck becomes empty, let $S$ be the sum of the values written on the cards on the board. Then, $S$ is the score of the game.

Little CS is very competitive by nature, and desires that his score is as great as possible. In fact, he wonders what is the greatest score he could achieve. That is, what is the highest value of $S$ that could be obtained by choosing $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_N$ optimally. Little CS also wonders what is the number of orders $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_N$ that lead to the highest value of $S$.

This is too easy of a task for Little CS, so instead, he decided to make it harder and give it to you. Therefore, he has chosen $N$ cards with values $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_N$ written on them, and $Q$ pairs of integers $(l, r)$ so that $1 \le l \le r \le N$, and for each one of them, he asks you to calculate the two values he wishes to find, if he would only play the game with the cards $a_l, a_{l+1}, \ldots a_r$.

## Input data

The first line of input contains $N$, the number of cards, and $Q$, the number of queries you are expected to answer. The second line contains $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_N$, the values written on Little CS' cards. Each of the following $Q$ lines contains two integers, the $i$-th line containing the $i$-th pair $(l_i, r_i)$ that Little CS has chosen for you.

## Output data

Each of the $Q$ lines of output must contain two space separated integers, representing the answer to Little CS' queries. More specifically, the $i$-th line must contain the following values in the given order:

• The maximum value of $S$ that could be obtained by playing only with the cards numbered from $l_i$ to $r_i$
• The number of arrays $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_{r_i - l_i + 1}$ that lead to the maximum score. Since this value could be quite large, you should output it modulo $10^{9} + 7$.

## Implementation details

You may use the following function while implementing your solution.

```C++
int product(int a, int b);
```

This will return, in constant time, the value $a \times (a + 1) \times \cdots \times (b - 1) \times b \bmod 10^{9} + 7$, i.e. the product of all integers between $a$ and $b$, modulo $10^{9} + 7$. Note that the parameters $a$ and $b$ need to satisfy $1 \le a \le b \le 200\,000$.

Remember to include the header `cards.h`, using the command `#include "cards.h"`! Note that you should still implement the `main` function.

problems.title: Ski Circuit
problems.problem:
After leaving Los Angeles, Little AD arrived in the Info(1)cup Ski Resort, the largest ski resort in the Info(1)cup Kingdom. The ski resort is made of $N + 1$ points numbered from 0 to $N$. The height of point $i$ is $H_i$, and $H_0 = 0$. There are no two points that have the same height.

For any two points $i$ and $j$ with $H_i < H_j$, there exists one chairlift that takes skiers from point $i$ to point $j$ and one slope that takes skiers from point $j$ to point $i$. Taking the slope from point $j$ to point $i$ takes exactly $H_j - H_i$ seconds. Please note that when taking the slope from point $j$ to point $i$, skiers are **not** required to visit all points $p$ with $H_i < H_p < H_j$. Moreover, when taking a chairlift from point $i$ to point $j$, skiers cannot stop at any point $p \ne j$.

It takes a skier $U_i$ seconds to get on a chairlift at point $i$ (regardless of where that chairlift goes) and $C_i$ seconds to get off a chairlift at point $i$ (regardless of where that chairlift comes from). $U_0 = C_0 = 0$.

Little AD wants to make a $K$-second circuit. That is, he wants to start from point 0, visit all the other $N$ points exactly once, and then return to point 0, and he wants to spend **at least** $K$ seconds on the slopes.

Little AD hates (as much as any proven skier) to stay in one point for too long. Therefore, let $W_i$ be the total time Little AD spends at point $i$, and let $M$ be the maximum value among all $W_i$. Note that $W_0 = 0$ and, for all $1 \le i \le N$:

• $W_i = 0$, if Little AD reaches point $i$ on a slope and leaves point $i$ on a slope,
• $W_i = C_i$, if Little AD reaches point $i$ with a chairlift and leaves point $i$ on a slope,
• $W_i = U_i$, if Little AD reaches point $i$ on a slope and leaves point $i$ with a chairlift,
• $W_i = U_i + C_i$ if Little AD reaches point $i$ with a chairlift and leaves point $i$ with a chairlift.

Now Little AD wonders: how much time does he need to spend in a single point so that he skis for a total of at least $K$ seconds? That is, what is the minimum value of $M$ he could achieve in order to spend at least $K$ seconds on the slopes?

Little AD needs your help! For $T$ given scenarios, you must find the minimum value of $M$ and help Little AD enjoy his well deserved ski holiday!

## Input data

The first line of input contains $T$, the number of scenarios your program will have to solve. For each of the $T$ scenarios, the first line will contain $N$ and $K$. The $i$-th of the following $N$ lines will contain three values $H_i$, $U_i$ and $C_i$. Please note that the input does not contain the values $H_0, U_0$ and $C_0$, since $H_0 = U_0 = C_0 = 0$.

## Output data

There should be exactly $T$ lines of output, with the $i$-th line of output containing the answer for the $i$-th scenario.

## Restrictions

• It is guaranteed that Little AD can ski at least $K$ seconds.
• $1 \le T \le 200$.
• Let $\sum N$ denote the sum of the values of $N$ for all scenarios.
• $1 \le \sum N \le 200\,000$.
• $1 \le K \le 10^{12}$
• $1 \le H_i, U_i, C_i \le 10^{6}$, for all $1 \le i \le N$

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \# & \text{Points} & \text{Restrictions} \\ \hline 1 & 6 & 1 \le \sum N \le 10 \\ 2 & 9 & 1 \le \sum N \le 17 \\ 3 & 19 & 1 \le \sum N \le 300 \\ 4 & 22 & 1 \le \sum N \le 2\,000 \\ 5 & 44 & \text{No further restrictions.} \end{array}$$

## Examples

```input
2
3 5
1 8 6
5 3 2
2 6 8
3 6
1 8 6
5 3 2
2 6 8
```

```output
2
8
```

## Explanations

**First scenario.** Little AD gets on the chairlift at point 0, then he gets off at point 2 and skies down to point 3. There he skies down to point 1, where he skies back to point 0.

$$W_0 = W_1 = W_3 = 0; W_2 = 2$$

**Second scenario.** Little AD gets on the chairlift at point 0 and goes up to point 2, where he gets off. Then he skies down to point 1. There he gets on the chairlift and goes up to point 3, where he gets down and skies back to point 0.

$$W_0 = 0; W_1 = W_3 = 8; W_2 = 2$$

problems.title: Modulosum
problems.problem:
C++ header: `modulosum.h`

The following problem was passed down through the generations in the Info(1)cup Kingdom — can you solve it?

You are given a sequence $A_0, \ldots, A_{N-1}$ of $N$ non-negative integers, and $Q$ queries of the form $(L_i, R_i, M_i)$ for $i = 0, \ldots, Q - 1$. For each query, compute

$$(A_{L_i} \bmod M_i) + \cdots + (A_{R_i} \bmod M_i).$$

For example, if $L = 2, R = 3, M = 5, A_2 = 3, A_3 = 4$, then the answer is $(3 \bmod 5) + (4 \bmod 5) = 7$.

## Implementation details

You should implement the following function.

```C++
std::vector <long long> solve(
    int N, int Q,
    std::vector<int> A,
    std::vector<int> L,
    std::vector<int> R,
    std::vector<int> M
);
```

This function should return the answer for the given $Q$ questions. It will only be called *once* per execution by the committee's grader. Note that the array $A$ is indexed from 0 to $N - 1$, and the arrays $L, R, M$ are indexed from 0 to $Q - 1$.

Remember to include the header `modulosum.h`! Also, remember that you *should not* implement the `main` function, only `solve`.

## Sample grader behaviour

The sample grader will read $N, Q$, the array $A$, and then $Q$ triplets $(L_i, R_i, M_i)$. It will then call `solve(N, Q, A, L, R, M)`, and output the returned values to standard output, one on a line. The input/output files below work for this grader.

## Restrictions

• $1 \le N \le 100\,000$
• $1 \le Q \le 100\,000$
• $0 \le L_i \le R_i < N$
• $1 \le M_i \le 1\,000\,000\,000$
• $1 \le A_i \le 300\,000$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \# & \text{Points} & \text{Restrictions} \\ \hline 1 & 8 & 1 \le N, Q \le 1\,000 \\ 2 & 5 & M_i = M_j,\ 1 \le i, j \le Q \\ 3 & 9 & 1 \le N \cdot M_i \le 2\,000\,000 \\ 4 & 11 & 1 \le N \cdot M_i \le 200\,000\,000 \\ 5 & 25 & 10\,000 \le M_i \\ 6 & 42 & \text{No further restrictions.} \end{array}$$

## Examples

```input

5 1 4 2 3
0 2 4
1 4 3
2 3 3
0 4 10
```

```output
2
4
3
15
```

In the first question, $(5 \bmod 4) + (1 \bmod 4) + (4 \bmod 4) = 1 + 1 + 0 = 2$.

In the second question, $(1 \bmod 3) + (4 \bmod 3) + (2 \bmod 3) + (3 \bmod 3) = 1 + 1 + 2 + 0 = 4$.

In the third question, $(4 \bmod 3) + (2 \bmod 3) = 1 + 2 = 3$.

In the fourth question,

$$(5 \bmod 10) + (1 \bmod 10) + (4 \bmod 10) + (2 \bmod 10) + (3 \bmod 10) = 5 + 1 + 4 + 2 + 3 = 15.$$

problems.title: Digit Sum
problems.problem:
Little Digit is, for whatever reason, interested in the sum of digits of numbers. For any non-negative integer $x$, let $\mathrm{DigitSum}(x)$ the sum of the digits of $x$. For example

$$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{DigitSum}(123) &= 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, \\ \mathrm{DigitSum}(998877) &= 9 + 9 + 8 + 8 + 7 + 7 = 48, \\ \mathrm{DigitSum}(0) &= 0. \end{aligned}$$

Her friend, Little Square, gave her an array $A_1, \ldots, A_N$ of $N$ non-negative integers, as well as another array $X_1, \ldots, X_Q$ of $Q$ non-negative integers. For every $i = 1, \ldots, Q$, help her find the sum

$$\mathrm{DigitSum}(X_i + A_1) + \cdots + \mathrm{DigitSum}(X_i + A_N).$$

## Input Data

The first line contains $N$ and $Q$. The next $N + Q$ lines contain the numbers $A_1, \ldots, A_N, X_1, \ldots, X_Q$, in that order, each on one line.

## Output

Output $Q$ lines. Line $i$ of the output should contain the sum

$$\mathrm{DigitSum}(X_i + A_1) + \cdots + \mathrm{DigitSum}(X_i + A_N).$$

## Restrictions

• $1 \le N, Q \le 5000$
• $1 \le A_i, X_i \le 10^{2000}$

$$\begin{array}{c|c|l} \# & \text{Points} & \text{Constraints} \\ \hline 1 & 19 & X_i, A_i \le 10^{9} \\ 2 & 18 & X_i, A_i \text{ consist only of digits } 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 \\ 3 & 15 & N, Q \le 300 \text{ and } X_i, A_i \le 10^{300} \\ 4 & 24 & N, Q \le 1000 \\ 5 & 24 & \text{No other restrictions} \end{array}$$

## Examples

```input
5 3
10
8
72
13
26
18
31
15
```

```output
39
41
42
```

## Explanations

The input is

$$\begin{aligned} A_1 &= 10, \\ A_2 &= 8, \\ A_3 &= 72, \\ A_4 &= 13, \\ A_5 &= 26 \end{aligned}$$

and

$$\begin{aligned} X_1 &= 18, \\ X_2 &= 31, \\ X_3 &= 15. \end{aligned}$$

We must compute 3 sums.

The first sum is

$$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{DigitSum}(X_1 + A_1) + \cdots + \mathrm{DigitSum}(X_1 + A_5) \\ &= \mathrm{DigitSum}(18 + 10) + \mathrm{DigitSum}(18 + 8) + \mathrm{DigitSum}(18 + 72) + \mathrm{DigitSum}(18 + 13) + \mathrm{DigitSum}(18 + 26) \\ &= \mathrm{DigitSum}(28) + \mathrm{DigitSum}(26) + \mathrm{DigitSum}(90) + \mathrm{DigitSum}(31) + \mathrm{DigitSum}(44) \\ &= 2 + 8 + 2 + 6 + 9 + 0 + 3 + 1 + 4 + 4 = 39. \end{aligned}$$

The second sum is

$$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{DigitSum}(X_2 + A_1) + \cdots + \mathrm{DigitSum}(X_2 + A_5) \\ &= \mathrm{DigitSum}(31 + 10) + \mathrm{DigitSum}(31 + 8) + \mathrm{DigitSum}(31 + 72) + \mathrm{DigitSum}(31 + 13) + \mathrm{DigitSum}(31 + 26) \\ &= \mathrm{DigitSum}(41) + \mathrm{DigitSum}(39) + \mathrm{DigitSum}(103) + \mathrm{DigitSum}(44) + \mathrm{DigitSum}(57) \\ &= 4 + 1 + 3 + 9 + 1 + 0 + 3 + 4 + 4 + 5 + 7 = 41. \end{aligned}$$

The third sum is

$$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{DigitSum}(X_3 + A_1) + \cdots + \mathrm{DigitSum}(X_3 + A_5) \\ &= \mathrm{DigitSum}(15 + 10) + \mathrm{DigitSum}(15 + 8) + \mathrm{DigitSum}(15 + 72) + \mathrm{DigitSum}(15 + 13) + \mathrm{DigitSum}(15 + 26) \\ &= \mathrm{DigitSum}(25) + \mathrm{DigitSum}(23) + \mathrm{DigitSum}(87) + \mathrm{DigitSum}(28) + \mathrm{DigitSum}(41) \\ &= 2 + 5 + 2 + 3 + 8 + 7 + 2 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 42. \end{aligned}$$

problems.title: Training
problems.problem:
The 2026 Foo(1)ball World Cup is approaching, and you, the Head Coach of the Info(1)Cup National Team, are preparing intense training sessions. Unfortunately, the hotel you booked has only one football pitch. After inspection, you find that the pitch has height $N$ meters and width $M$ meters. That would be perfectly fine if $N$ and $M$ had proper proportions. The issue is that $\underline{N \le 3}$ while $M \le 200\,000$.

Each of the $N \times M$ players is placed at a distinct position $(i, j)$ on the pitch, where $1 \le i \le N$ and $1 \le j \le M$. Each player belongs to exactly one team; let $A_{i,j}$ denote the team of the player at position $(i, j)$.

You have two assistants with very different philosophies: Attack and Defense. They prepared the following game, which is played *independently for each team*.

• 1. Defense chooses one player of the team who receives the ball first.
• 2. Then, the assistants alternate turns. Attack moves first, followed by Defense, and so on.
• 3. On a turn, the current assistant chooses the player who currently has the ball and tells them to which player the ball should be passed. **This player must be from the same team.**
• 4. Since the players are not in the best shape, a player may only pass the ball to a teammate who is located either in the same row or in the same column of the pitch.
• 5. Due to exhaustion, if a player receives the ball more than once, they will get injured. The assistants will never choose this option, as it is strongly against the team's interests.
• 6. When the current player has no one to pass the ball to, the assistant whose turn it is loses the game.

Both assistants play optimally.

You want to test how players adapt in different situations, so you perform $Q$ substitutions. Each substitution has the following form:

The player at position $(x, y)$ is assigned to team $t$.

That is, we set $A_{x,y}$ to $t$. (It is possible that $A_{x,y}$ was already equal to $t$.)

Before any substitutions, and after each substitution, determine the number of teams for which Attack wins the game.

## Input Data

The first line contains $N$ and $M$. The next $N$ lines contain $M$ elements each. On the $i$-th of these lines, the $j$-th value is $A_{i,j}$. The next line contains the value $Q$. The following $Q$ lines each contain three integers: $x$, $y$, and $t$.

## Output Data

Output $Q + 1$ lines. The first line should contain the number of winning teams for Attack before any substitutions. The $i + 1$-th line should contain the number of winning teams for Attack after the $i$-th substitution.

## Restrictions

• $1 \le N \le 3$
• $1 \le M, Q \le 200\,000$
• $1 \le N \times M \le 200\,000$
• $1 \le A_{i,j} \le N \times M$
• For every substitution: $1 \le x \le N, 1 \le y \le M, 1 \le t \le N \times M$

$$\begin{array}{c|c|l} \# & \text{Points} & \text{Constraints} \\ \hline 1 & 19 & N = 1,\ Q \le 100 \\ 2 & 20 & N = 1 \\ 3 & 8 & M = 3 \\ 4 & 18 & N = 2,\ Q \le 100 \\ 5 & 17 & N = 2 \\ 6 & 18 & \text{No further restrictions} \end{array}$$

## Examples

### Example 1

```input
1 6
1 2 2 1 2 1
3
1 1 2
1 2 3
1 1 3
```

```output
0
2
1
3
```

### Example 2

```input
2 4
1 2 3 1
2 2 2 3
3
1 4 2
1 2 1
2 4 1
```

```output
2
0
1
0
```

### Example 3

```input
3 3
3 9 1
9 3 3
3 9 9
3
2 1 3
2 3 9
3 3 1
```

```output
1
0
2
2
```

## Explanations

Let's look at the first sample. Before making any substitutions, Defense can win the game for both teams. For example, let's analyze team 1:

Suppose Defense gives the ball to the player standing at $(1, 4)$. Then, Attack makes the player at $(1, 4)$ pass the ball to the player at $(1, 1)$. Now, the only option for Defense is to make the player at $(1, 1)$ pass the ball to the player at $(1, 6)$. Since there are no other players in team 1, the player at $(1, 6)$ cannot pass the ball to anyone else. Since it is Attack's turn, they lose.

After the first substitution, the pitch looks as follows:

```
2 2 2 1 2 1
```

For team 1, if Defense gives the ball to the player at $(1, 4)$, Attack can make them pass the ball to $(1, 6)$. Now, there is nowhere to pass the ball. Hence, Attack wins the game for team 1.

problems.title: Triangulation
problems.problem:
Little Polygon received a gift from his wonderful friend Little Circle. In the gift there was a drawing of an $N$ vertex polygon, each vertex being labeled with an integer from 1 to $N$, and a triangulation of it, e.g:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/informatics-olympiads-bank/main/images/info1cup-2026-1-3-fig1.png

There was also a note, which asked Little Polygon to write every number from 2 to $N - 1$ once, one number inside each triangle, so that number $i$ is written in a triangle that has vertex $i$ as a corner. For example:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/informatics-olympiads-bank/main/images/info1cup-2026-1-3-fig2.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/informatics-olympiads-bank/main/images/info1cup-2026-1-3-fig3.png

Help Little Polygon find a way of writing these numbers inside the triangles, as well as counting how many ways of doing this there are.

problems.title: Grow Gravity
problems.problem:
Little Newton likes gravity and plays with a magical shape made out of $1 \times 1$ squares, suspended in the air.

Initially, this shape is made of only one such square. On this magical shape two things happen (in this order):

• 1. Grow phase: Around each square in this shape some new squares will appear. The grow phase can be of two types:
◦ **Type +.** The new squares will appear around the squares in only 4 directions (north, south, east and west).
◦ **Type \*.** The new squares will appear in 8 directions (north, south, east, west, north-east, north-west, south-east and south-west).
• 2. Gravity phase: In this phase, Little Newton places a plate under the shape and lets all the squares fall onto it. **Note:** The plate is removed immediately after this operation!

As an example, the effects of each of the 2 types of grow phases, followed by a gravity phase, are pictured below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/informatics-olympiads-bank/main/images/info1cup-2026-2-1-fig1.png

Little Newton has an array $v_1, \ldots, v_N$ of $N$ types of grow phases and wants to do $Q$ operations of the following types:

• $\mathrm{update}(i)$: If $v_i = +$ then set it to $\star$; otherwise if $v_i = \star$ set it to $+$.
• $\mathrm{query}(\ell, r)$: Suppose Little Newton starts with a shape made out of only one $1 \times 1$ square and applies, for $i = \ell, \ldots, r$, in order, a grow phase of type $v_i$ followed by a gravity phase. How many $1 \times 1$ squares will the shape have in the end?

Help Little Newton answer all of these queries.

## Input data

The first line of the input contains the number $N$. The second line contains $N$ symbols from among $\{+, \star\}$, not separated by spaces, representing the initial values of $v_1, \ldots, v_N$. The third line of the input contains the number $Q$. Then, each of the following $Q$ lines will contain one of the following: either two integers $1\ i$ representing an $\mathrm{update}(i)$ operation, or three integers $2\ \ell\ r$ representing a $\mathrm{query}(\ell, r)$ operation.

## Output data

You should output the answer for each $\mathrm{query}(\ell, r)$ operation, each on a new line.

## Restrictions

• $1 \le N \le 200\,000$.
• $1 \le Q \le 200\,000$.
• $v_i \in \{+, \star\}$ for $1 \le i \le N$.
• $t \in \{1, 2\}$, $1 \le i \le N$ and $1 \le \ell \le r \le N$ for each operation.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|l} \# & \text{Points} & \text{Constraints} \\ \hline 1 & 5 & v_i = \star \text{ for each } 1 \le i \le N \text{ and the operations are only of type 2.} \\ 2 & 10 & 1 \le N \le 40 \text{ and } 1 \le Q \le 40. \\ 3 & 20 & 1 \le N \le 300 \text{ and } 1 \le Q \le 300. \\ 4 & 30 & v_i = + \text{ for each } 1 \le i \le N \text{ and the operations are only of type 2.} \\ 5 & 35 & \text{No further restrictions.} \end{array}$$

## Examples

```input
4
+*++
9
2 2 4
1 3
1 4
2 2 4
1 1
1 2
1 3
1 4
2 2 4
```

```output
39
49
31
```

## Explanations

**First query.** In this query, the sequence of operations is $\star{+}{+}$. The shape thus has the following configurations.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/informatics-olympiads-bank/main/images/info1cup-2026-2-1-fig2.png

Hence the answer is 39.

**Second query.** In the second query, the sequence of operations is $\star\star\star$. The shape thus has the following configurations.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/informatics-olympiads-bank/main/images/info1cup-2026-2-1-fig3.png

Therefore, the answer is 49.

**Third query.** In the last query, the sequence of operations is ${+}{+}{+}$. The shape thus has the following configurations.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/informatics-olympiads-bank/main/images/info1cup-2026-2-1-fig4.png

Thus, the answer is 31.

problems.title: Hearts
problems.problem:
Little Green Heart has gifted Little Purple Heart for Valentine's Day two arrays $A$ and $B$ of size $N$ which together contain the numbers from 1 to $2 \times N$ exactly once.

Little Purple Heart performs the following operation:

• 1. She chooses 2 indices $l$ and $r$ with $1 \le l \le r \le N$.
• 2. She creates an array $C$ of size $k = r - l + 1$, such that for every $i$ with $0 \le i < k$ she chooses either $C_i = A_{l+i}$ or $C_i = B_{l+i}$.
• 3. She calculates the value $\mathrm{val}(C)$, which is equal to the number of indices $i$ with $0 \le i < k$ such that there is no index $j$ with $0 \le j < i$ and $C_j > C_i$.

Little Green Heart, being the computer scientist that he is, wants to impress Little Purple Heart by computing the sum of $\mathrm{val}(C)$ for all the arrays $C$ that she could have constructed. Since this number can be quite large, he wants to compute it modulo $10^{9} + 7$. Moreover, he wants to do so for $Q$ different operations.

Formally, given $Q$ queries of the form $(l, r)$, $1 \le l \le r \le N$, he defines $S$ as the set of all the arrays $C$ that Little Purple Heart could have built. Then, for each query, he wants to calculate

$$P(l, r) = \sum_{C \in S} \mathrm{val}(C) \mod 10^{9} + 7$$

Your task is to help Little Green Heart impress Little Purple Heart by computing the answer to each query.

## Input data

The first line of the input contains the number $N$. The second line contains $N$ numbers $A_1, A_2, \ldots A_n$ representing the array $A$. The third line contains $N$ numbers $B_1, B_2, \ldots B_n$ representing the array $B$. Together, these 2 arrays contain the numbers from 1 to $2 \times N$ exactly once.

The fourth line contains the number of queries $Q$. Each of the following $Q$ lines contains 2 numbers describing a query of the form $l\ r$.

## Output data

The output should contain $Q$ lines representing the answers to all queries $P(l, r)$, each on a new line, computed modulo $10^{9} + 7$.

## Restrictions

• $1 \le N \le 70\,000$.
• $1 \le Q \le 70\,000$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|l} \# & \text{Points} & \text{Constraints} \\ \hline 1 & 5 & 1 \le N \le 17,\ 1 \le Q \le 100 \\ 2 & 16 & 1 \le N, Q \le 300 \\ 3 & 9 & B_i = A_i + 1 \text{ for all } i \text{ with } 1 \le i \le N \\ 4 & 17 & 1 \le N, Q \le 10\,000 \\ 5 & 11 & 1 \le Q \le 200 \\ 6 & 14 & 1 \le N \le 50\,000,\ 1 \le Q \le 10\,000 \\ 7 & 10 & 1 \le N, Q \le 50\,000 \\ 8 & 18 & \text{No further restrictions} \end{array}$$

## Examples

### Example 1

```input
6
2 10 3 4 5 6
11 1 9 8 7 12
2
3 6
1 2
```

```output
37
5
```

### Example 2

```input
12
11 10 7 23 1 18 22 16 8 14 20 6
3 4 9 13 19 5 24 12 15 21 17 2
1
7 11
```

```output
32
```

## Explanations

**First example.** There are 2 queries.

For the first query, we will consider the subsequences $A_3, A_4, A_5, A_6$ and $B_3, B_4, B_5, B_6$ when constructing $C$. Next we consider all possible options for $C$ and sum $\mathrm{val}(C)$. For example, for $C = [3, 8, 7, 12]$, the indexes $i = 0, 1, 3$ have the property that there is no $0 \le j < i$ such that $C_j > C_i$. Therefore, $\mathrm{val}(C) = 3$.

Summing $\mathrm{val}(C)$ across all arrays $C$ that can be constructed, we get $P(3, 6) = 37$.

For the second query, we can construct 4 arrays $C$:

$P(1, 2) = \mathrm{val}([2, 10]) + \mathrm{val}([2, 1]) + \mathrm{val}([11, 10]) + \mathrm{val}([11, 1]) = 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 5$.

**Second example.** There is one query. Computing $P(7, 11) = 32$.

problems.title: Trees
problems.problem:
Little Tree is interested in trees of various sizes. She has a rooted binary tree $T$ (i.e. one where every vertex has at most 2 children), *not necessarily a balanced tree*, in front of her, whose root is denoted by 1 and whose vertices are labeled $1, \ldots, 2^{N}$. The label of any vertex is always strictly less than any of its children.

A set of vertices $S$ is called *valid* if no vertex in $S$ is the ancestor of any other vertex in $S$. The value of $S$, denoted by $\mathrm{val}(S)$, is given by the number of vertices within the tree that have *any* vertex of $S$ as an ancestor. (We consider a node to be its own ancestor.) In other words, it is the sum of the sizes of the subtrees rooted at vertices in $S$.

Her enemy, Little Cactus, challenges her to the following task: Given $N$ and the tree $T$, create as many *valid, nonempty* sets $S_1, \ldots, S_K$ as possible, such that

$$|S_1| + \cdots + |S_K| \le N \times 2^{N-1} + 1$$

and $\mathrm{val}(S_i) \ne \mathrm{val}(S_j)$ for any $i \ne j$.

## Input data

The first line of the input file contains the integer $N$. The second line contains integers $p_2, \ldots, p_{2^N}$, separated by spaces, where $p_i$ denotes the parent of node $i$.

## Output data

Output $K$, the number of sets you can create, followed by each of the $K$ sets on its own line. To output a set, first output its size, then its elements, separated by spaces.

## Restrictions

• $N \le 18$.
• If you output an incorrect solution (i.e. one using too many vertices, or where two sets have the same value) then you will receive 0 points for a test. Otherwise, the fraction of the score you will receive for a particular test will be equal to $(K / 2^{N})^{1.5}$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|l} \# & \text{Points} & \text{Constraints} \\ \hline 1 & 7 & p_i = i - 1 \text{ for } i = 2, \ldots, 2^{N} \\ 2 & 12 & N = 4 \\ 3 & 13 & N = 6 \\ 4 & 21 & N = 9 \\ 5 & 26 & N = 11 \\ 6 & 21 & \text{No further restrictions} \end{array}$$

## Examples

### Example 1

```input
2
1 2 3
```

```output
4
1 4
1 3
1 2
1 1
```

### Example 2

```input
2
1 2 2
```

```output
4
1 4
2 3 4
1 2
1 1
```

## Explanation

**First case.** The tree is given by

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/informatics-olympiads-bank/main/images/info1cup-2026-2-3-fig1.png

We see that the sets $S_1 = \{4\}, S_2 = \{3\}, S_3 = \{2\}, S_4 = \{1\}$ all have distinct values (namely 1, 2, 3, 4 respectively), and have total size $4 \le 2 \times 2^{2-1} + 1 = 5$. Hence this output is correct.

**Second case.** The tree is given by

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/informatics-olympiads-bank/main/images/info1cup-2026-2-3-fig2.png

We see that the sets $S_1 = \{4\}, S_2 = \{3, 4\}, S_3 = \{2\}, S_4 = \{1\}$ all have distinct values (namely 1, 2, 3, 4 respectively), and have total size $5 \le 2 \times 2^{2-1} + 1 = 5$. Hence this output is correct.
